profiles.meeting_scenario: A preoperative planning meeting at a tertiary spine center for a 64-year-old man with multilevel cervical spondylotic myelopathy, progressive hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, and severe canal stenosis from C3 to C6. The agenda is to confirm readiness for a planned posterior cervical decompression and fusion scheduled for next Thursday, align on what needs to be in the chart before surgery, and assign who will finalize imaging, documentation, and OR logistics. The expected outcome is a shared plan for case booking, pre-op documentation, equipment preparation, and timeline to keep the operation on schedule.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Cervical degenerative disease surgery, deformity planning, operative decision-making
members.background: An orthopedic spine surgeon with 12 years in academic practice who routinely performs multilevel cervical decompressions and relies on established clinic-to-OR workflows.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid delays or rework that could push the case off next week's schedule, and she prefers not to reopen settled planning details unless something clearly changes the surgical indication.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to 'the January MRI,' they mean the 1/12 outside diagnostic MRI she personally reviewed in clinic and used to decide on surgery.
'Medically cleared' means the patient's PCP and cardiology consultants have already said no further pre-op optimization is needed, even if ancillary items are still filtering into the chart.

'Standard posterior cervical set-up' for her usual cases implicitly includes Mayfield fixation, neuromonitoring, cell saver, an O-arm spin, and backup fixation options if bone quality is worse than expected.
Her clinic neurological exam from last week is an adequate baseline for postoperative comparison unless there has been a major interval change.

members.name: Jordan Ruiz
members.role: Spine physician assistant and perioperative coordinator
members.expertise: Pre-op workflow management, surgical scheduling, documentation pathways, inpatient spine care
members.background: A PA who coordinates the cervical spine service's operative cases, manages chart readiness, communicates with anesthesia and OR staff, and translates surgeon plans into executable logistics.
members.private_state: He wants a frictionless day-of-surgery workflow with no missing chart items, equipment surprises, or documentation gaps that create nursing or anesthesia escalations.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'the January MRI,' they usually mean the most recent January study available in the health system chart, which in this case is the 1/29 repeat MRI.
'Medically cleared' means all required clearance components are complete in the chart: anesthesia visit, labs, EKG, consultant notes, and medication-hold instructions.
'Standard posterior cervical set-up' means the existing preference card only, unless extra equipment or backup implants are explicitly requested for this specific case.
A 'baseline neuro exam' should be a fresh pre-op or day-before structured note with detailed motor grading and functional elements that downstream teams can use directly.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'January MRI' is the operative reference
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer casually to 'the January MRI' or 'the January scan.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the 1/12 outside-hospital cervical MRI that established the operative levels in clinic.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the 1/29 in-system repeat MRI that is the most recent January scan in the chart packet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both scans are indeed from January, both are cervical MRIs on the same patient, and the meeting is about logistics rather than re-debating the operative indication, so the phrase feels precise enough to neither of them.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the patient is or will be 'medically cleared' before surgery.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the PCP and cardiologist have already indicated the patient can proceed without additional workup.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the chart will contain the full operational clearance package, including anesthesia review, uploaded tests, and medication instructions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In perioperative medicine, 'cleared' is commonly used as shorthand for several related readiness states, so both hear it as routine confirmation rather than as a term needing unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'standard posterior cervical set-up'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use the 'standard posterior cervical set-up' for the case.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes her usual extras for multilevel cervical myelopathy cases: Mayfield, neuromonitoring, cell saver, O-arm, and backup fixation inventory beyond the default tray.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes only what is already on the posted standard preference card for posterior cervical fusion unless separately specified.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds routine and institutionally standardized, so neither expects that the other is mentally bundling a different set of implicit add-ons into the same label.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say a 'baseline neuro exam' should be in place before surgery.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes her clinic exam from last week is sufficient because it documents the deficits relevant to postoperative comparison.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes a fresh structured pre-op note is needed to count as the usable baseline for pathway compliance and inpatient handoff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the importance of having a baseline exam, but their threshold for when that requirement is fulfilled differs in a way that usually stays invisible until someone tries to close the chart or build the handoff note.
